content: Dana Reyes is the tech lead of the Atlas web app at Northwind Robotics.
Atlas is written in TypeScript with a Next.js frontend and a FastAPI backend.
The Atlas production database is PostgreSQL 16 hosted on Neon.
Dana prefers tabs over spaces and a 100 character line limit.
All Atlas pull requests need one approving review from Priya Natarajan before merge.
The Atlas staging environment lives at staging.atlas.example and deploys from the develop branch.
Atlas uses Stripe for billing; webhooks are verified with the signing secret stored in Vault.
Never run database migrations on Atlas during business hours; the window is 02:00 to 04:00 UTC.
The Atlas test suite runs with pnpm test and takes about nine minutes in CI.
Marcus Bell owns the Atlas design system and the Figma component library.
Atlas authentication uses Auth0 with passwordless email login.
Atlas authentication moved from Auth0 to Clerk; passwordless email login is unchanged.
The Atlas release cadence is every second Tuesday.
The Atlas release cadence changed to weekly, every Thursday.
Atlas error tracking is handled by Sentry and alerts go to the #atlas-alerts Slack channel.
The Atlas API rate limit is 60 requests per minute per API key.
The Atlas API rate limit was raised to 120 requests per minute per API key.
Dana's working hours are 9am to 5pm Eastern, and she is offline on Fridays.
Feature flags in Atlas are managed with LaunchDarkly; the flag prefix is atlas_.
The Atlas search feature is backed by Meilisearch running on a single 4 GB instance.
Customer Globex reported that CSV export times out for reports above 50,000 rows.
The CSV export timeout for Globex was fixed by streaming the response; shipped in release 4.12.
The Atlas on-call rotation is weekly and hands over on Monday at 10:00 Eastern.
Priya Natarajan is the security reviewer for anything touching authentication or payments.
The Atlas mobile client is a React Native app maintained by Tomasz Zielinski.
Images uploaded to Atlas are stored in the S3 bucket atlas-media-prod with a 90 day lifecycle rule for originals.
Dana wants commit messages in the imperative mood with the ticket number as a prefix.
The Atlas backend runs on Python 3.11.
The Atlas backend was upgraded to Python 3.13 last sprint.
The primary Atlas contact at Globex is Elena Vasquez.
Elena Vasquez left Globex; the new Atlas contact there is Raj Patel.
Atlas background jobs run on Celery with Redis as the broker.
The Atlas analytics dashboard queries a read replica, never the primary database.
Dana dislikes long meetings and prefers written updates in the weekly doc.
The Atlas pricing page copy is owned by marketing; engineers must not edit it without sign-off from Lena Okafor.
Accessibility target for Atlas is WCAG 2.2 AA, audited each quarter.
The Atlas monorepo uses Turborepo and pnpm workspaces.
Load testing showed Atlas handles 800 concurrent users before p95 latency exceeds one second.
The Atlas CI pipeline runs on GitHub Actions with self-hosted runners for the end-to-end tests.
Tomasz is on parental leave until the end of January; Ines Moreau covers the mobile client.
The decision was made to drop Internet Explorer and legacy Edge support in Atlas.
Atlas email is sent through Postmark; the transactional stream is separate from the broadcast stream.
The Atlas data retention policy deletes inactive accounts after 24 months.
Dana's dog is a border collie named Juniper.
Dana is allergic to peanuts, so team lunches must avoid Thai and satay dishes.
The quarterly planning offsite is in Lisbon during the first week of March.
A temporary promo code LAUNCH25 gives new Atlas customers 25 percent off.
The Atlas staging database is frozen for the audit and must not be written to.
Ines found that the Android build fails on Gradle 9 because of the camera plugin.
The Atlas onboarding flow conversion rate rose from 31 percent to 38 percent after the checklist redesign.
Next step for Atlas: finish the invoice PDF renderer and add tests for multi-currency totals.
Open bug: the Atlas notification bell shows a stale unread count after marking all as read.
Harbor is the nightly data pipeline that loads warehouse telemetry into BigQuery.
Harbor is written in Python and orchestrated by Dagster.
The Harbor production database is ClickHouse for hot data, with BigQuery as the archive.
Kofi Mensah is the tech lead of the Harbor pipeline.
Harbor pull requests need two approving reviews, one of them from Kofi Mensah.
The Harbor API rate limit is 600 requests per minute per service account.
Harbor authentication uses Google service accounts with workload identity federation.
The Harbor release cadence is continuous; every merge to main deploys.
Harbor error tracking is handled by Datadog and pages go through PagerDuty.
The Harbor nightly run starts at 01:30 UTC and must finish before 05:00 UTC.
Sensor readings older than 13 months are moved from ClickHouse to cold storage.
The Harbor test suite runs with pytest and takes about four minutes.
Harbor deduplicates telemetry events by device id and event timestamp.
Warehouse 7 in Rotterdam sends malformed timestamps every time its gateway restarts.
The Harbor schema registry lives in the harbor-schemas repository and uses Avro.
Harbor backfills are limited to seven days at a time to protect the ClickHouse cluster.
The BigQuery monthly budget for Harbor is 4,000 dollars; an alert fires at 80 percent.
Kofi prefers that Harbor incidents get a written postmortem within three working days.
Harbor uses dbt for the transformation layer, with models tagged by warehouse region.
The Harbor staging environment runs against a sampled one percent dataset.
Yuki Tanaka maintains the Harbor ingestion gateway written in Go.
A Harbor job failed three nights in a row because the Rotterdam partition was missing.
The missing Rotterdam partition was caused by a renamed bucket; the path is now parameterised.
Harbor secrets are stored in Google Secret Manager and rotated every 90 days.
Next step for Harbor: add row count checks between ClickHouse and BigQuery after each nightly load.
Harbor cost review found that 40 percent of BigQuery spend comes from one unpartitioned table.
